title: Building Gentlemen at Home How Manners Form Character
author: Chris Martin
source: The Ways of a Gentleman (Martin Substack), February 5, 2026
summary: Martin argues that in an age of social media and reality television, parents and mentors must proactively teach young men the habits of character through manners and etiquette—not as snobbish superiority but as the visible expression of inner virtue. Manners matter because they teach discipline, respect, and leadership. Martin organizes character formation around three arenas: the dinner table (where civility begins, through self-control and gratitude), conduct about town (where everyday courtesies and steady presence demonstrate dignity), and behavior with women (where respect and attentiveness prepare boys for honorable manhood). The central thesis is that manners are not superficial—they are the concrete practices through which boys learn self-respect, learn to serve, and learn to carry themselves with strength and grace.
points: Character starts with respect for oneself and others, and it is manifested in conduct—manners are not superficial, they are the visible expression of inner virtue.

When a boy learns to respect others he learns discipline; when he learns to serve others he learns leadership; when he learns to carry himself with dignity he learns self-respect—these lessons shape every arena of a man's life.
The dinner table is a mirror of a man's character: how he eats reveals how he treats people in other settings, and mealtime teaches self-control, respect, and grace under pressure.

A gentleman's everyday presence comes from consistently practicing small courtesies—holding doors, proper greeting, restrained speech—which develop not just social skill but genuine confidence rooted in humility.

Chivalry is not dead and is not weakness; young men must learn that showing honor and respect toward women through thoughtful planning, sincere speech, and attentiveness teaches empathy and prepares them for honorable leadership in marriage and family.
quotes: Each generation faces unique conditions that shape the identity of young people. Today, young men and women come of age in a world shaped by social media and reality television. Now more than ever, we must fight against these notions and proactively teach young men how to live a life of character.
Character starts with respect for one's self and respect for others, and it is manifested in one's conduct. Manners matter, and they not only benefit young men, they benefit society as a whole.
In my opinion, the dinner table is a mirror of a man's character. How he eats and conducts himself in the company of others usually reveals how he treats people in other settings.

When a young man learns to sit upright, place his napkin in his lap, wait for others to be served, and express gratitude to his host, he's learning far more than table manners. He is learning self-control and respect.
The true measure of a man isn't how he behaves when people are watching, but how he acts in everyday life. These lessons teach young men that dignity is something you demonstrate on a daily basis.

Few moments reveal a man's character more than how he treats women. Chivalry is not dead, and young men must learn that it is not a weakness. It's about respecting women of all ages, and showing them consideration throughout one's life.” Archived from The Ways of a Gentleman (Martin Substack) on May 2, 2026 by Tim.
